newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First's Peters says 0-2 pct target critical.
newsitem.headline: NZ First's Peters says 0-2 pct target critical.

text.p: NZ First leader Winston Peters said on Tuesday that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's 0-2 percent inflation target was wrong and that it was a critical issue.
His party holds the balance of power since the inconclusive October 12 election and has been in coalition talks with the centre-left Labour Party and the caretaker conservative National Party.
"I think it is a very critical issue I think there is a growing trend of economic expertise that has learnt to question whether that is the right target," he told Radio New Zealand.
"In the last the year or so as the dollar has trended upwards and more and more people and more and more opinion has come on side to the view that we may have the wrong target here," he said.

Peters was asked about a speech delivered by RBNZ Governor Don Brash on Monday where Brash warned that next year's tax cuts may have to be deferred if plans by political parties continued to put pressure on monetary policy and the New Zealand dollar.
Peters though said the Reserve Bank's policy was bad for trade and bad for exporters.
"We should have a target that is set higher than that (02 percent)... a target below the average of our trading partners."
He asked why 0-2 percent was magical.
However, Peters said he was unconcerned about Brash's comments with respect to deferring the tax cuts.
"It has no effect on our policy because we intend to take those tax cuts and use them for a compulsory savings regime which is anti-inflationary."
Peters said the issue of a compulsoary pension scheme was being discussed as an issue in talks with other parties.
He said there would be new spending in areas of social welfare and education.
"I don't think anybody expects things to carry on as they were before."
Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said he believed Brash's comments were directed at all parties.
He noted that New Zealand was running the highest surplus in the Western World
"So clearly therefore the answer to the high exchange rate is not to run higher and higher surpluses."
He said the answer had to come to other areas of economic policy to look at the answer for the imbalance in monetary and fiscal policies.

"I would hope that the markets would focus on what was new in what Dr Brash was saying which was that the exchange rate is over valued, the Reserve Bank recognises that fact and would therefore like to see that exchange rate come down in the very near future," he said.
"I think it is in part one of Dr Brash's subtle signals," he said.
Cullen said that as far as he was aware all the parties were still talking in terms of reasonably strong fiscal surpluses next year and so that was not the reason why interest rates were so high.
Cullen said a reason for the high dollar was foreign investors could invest with "excessive certainty about Reserve Bank policy with respect to the future of the exchange rate".
